newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: OPINION - IMPORTED S.AFRICAN INFLATION - BY E.OSBORN.
newsitem.headline: OPINION - IMPORTED S.AFRICAN INFLATION - BY E.OSBORN.

text.p: By Edward Osborn, consultant to Edey, Rogers (Pty) Ltd

On the same day that the producer price index (PPI) for September was published, showing negligible imported inflation, the minister of trade and industry was reported as saying imported prices were rising.
Indeed the PPI figures were once again treated with cold sceptism as inadequately reflecting what must be taking place with the price of imported commodities because of the falling rand.

The lack of sensitivity of the PPI figures to the value of the rand was highlighted in the new table published by the Central Statistical Service with details on price movements for imported commodities in August and September.

Of the 33 categories zero price change was reflected in both August and September in 21 categories and a common 18 categories showed no change whatsoever in the two months. Overall the imported index increased by 0.1 percent in both August and September. Furthermore the increase in September over the past twelve months was but 4.7 percent.

A trade weighted index of exchange rates against the rand reflects a 3.3 percent depreciation in August but a strengthening of 2.4 percent in September. The twelve month depreciation of the rand has been 17.1 percent to September. The currency collapse and turbulence has not been reflected in the PPI and clearly the official PPI is inadequately measuring imported inflaton.

There have been sweeping explanations thumb-sucked to reconcile the two, embracing the counter-effects of reduced tariffs, the removal of the surcharges in October 1995 - which would imply a sizeable kick-up when it comes to the anniversary PPI for October 1996 - and the rewards of heightened competition in the South African economy. All these imply the correctness of the PPI and that there has indeed been negligible imported inflation into South Africa.

The problem has not been confined to 1996. It has simply become noticeable and puzzling in the face of what has happened to the exchange rates this year. After high imported inflation figures for a number of years through to 1990, the imported inflation figures have been consistently low since. Just taking the December to December rises the increase was 1.9 percent in 1991, then successively 3.1 percent, 4.1 percent, 6.9 percent, 5.7 percent to December 1995. This is a a cumulative rise in imported prices of 23.5 percent in the five years, as compared with a rand depreciation of 30.5 percent and an increase of unit value of imports, f.o.b., of 39 percent in the time.

In a letter to Business Day of September 11 the head of the CSS, Mark Orkin, points out that contrary to common supposition prices of the imported commodities are obtained directly from respondents. They are not based on Customs and Excise import data with the sole exception of crude oil and therefore faulty and suspect trade data are not to blame for any assumed inaccuracy in the PPI. With a hint of asperity he ended his letter by questioning the quality of economic commentary.

Economic commentary may well be poor, hasty, or superficial but the point still remains that the story as told by the PPI differs from what one would expect naturally, whether one is an economist or not. As a statistician Orkin would know that the statistics diverging from or not reflecting experience are either suspect or in need of special justification, so he should not be too hard on us ignorant economists floundering about for explanations. One must compliment him though on his refreshing efforts to explain apparent anomalies to the public, as in the case of the peculiar oil price in the PPI figures.
There still remains the apparent anomaly of the lack of sensitivity of the import component of the PPI to the rand weakness.

On closer examination of the compilation of the data there are a number of explanations that can be advanced. They are straightforward and acceptable and suggest nothing untoward about the accuracy of the figures. After all, as Orkin says, the PPI is prepared with enormous care and detail.

The first point to make is that the price of the imported commodities are the selling prices of goods that have been imported by the respondents. This is fundamental in that the commodities may have been imported at any time in the past and are not confined to current imports. It is the selling price of the respondent that is current.

Secondly, prices reported have to be in respect of the same specific commodity in terms of type, quality and model. A zero change in price can therefore either reflect just that or the fact that the identical commodity was not available for sale in the current month. It is possible that suppliers of imported commodities can maintain their selling prices unchanged for contractual or marketing reasons notwithstanding an increase in the landed costs; they would be carrying the higher costs until such time as a change in selling price is made.
In the case of identical items not being sold in the current month, the price is kept on record until again available when the full change, if any, will be recorded in the relevant current month.

The implication of these simple characteristics is that currency movements will not necessarily have any immediate bearing on import prices in the PPI. The effects could be delayed, and because of the problems of comparability there could be delayed spiking of price changes. Competition can also play a part in suppressing the effects of currency movements.

Nevertheless the PPI should reflect the broad movement of landed import costs over time. Naturally these landed costs will be affected by currency movements, the basic international price movements and changes to tarrif and surcharge structure. Where we have erred is expecting an immediacy of currency movements into the PPI. Furthermore the current lack of movement of the price of imported commodities is perfectly compatible with the minister's statement about higher costs of importing raw materials for production.

Imported goods going directly to production (eg raw materials, machinery, components for assembly) will have their cost effects transmitted to end-prices in time, but imported goods for onward sale are not necessarily reflecting an immediate impact on the PPI because of the methodology of comparibility and possibly because of the absorption of higher costs by the distributor. But certainly in practice the PPI is not showing the same movement of import prices generally.
(The opinions expressed in this article represent those of the author only. They should not be seen to represent the views of Reuters.)
